newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian call rates subdued despite huge outflows.
newsitem.headline: Indian call rates subdued despite huge outflows.

text.p: Indian call rates have been subdued despite a substantial drain of funds from the banking system this month, bank dealers said on Friday.

Call rates opened at 0.25-0.50 percent on reporting Friday for banks, when there is little demand for money. Overnight rates closed at 10.25-10.50 percent on Thursday, down from a high of 10.50-10.75 percent seen through the week.
"Call money is behaving rationally compared to last September, when it touched three-digit levels," said a dealer, referring to days of acute shortage of funds last year.
These rates have tested 11.0 percent level in recent months, the rate at which the Reserve Bank of India gives concessional export credit, but did not cross this barrier.

"The amount of tax outflows this year is substantially higher compared to last year because of the minimum alternate tax (MAT) imposed by the government," said R. Narayan, assistant treasury manager at the Bombay branch of Bank of Nova Scotia.
The government imposed MAT in its July budget, bringing leading Indian firms which have not been paying corporate tax under the tax net for the first time.
Bankers expect tax payments by Indian firms to the exchequer at 50-60 billion rupees this year compared to 40-50 billion rupees last year.
Another 12.5 billion rupees left the banking system this week, being the fourth instalment of the 13.85 percent government stock maturing in 2006.
The government has kept up its market borrowing in recent months. The finance ministry has announced a sale of 20 billion rupees of government stock on October 7.
Government debt has been attracting much buying interest in recent weeks, with banks funding these purchases out of call funds, a bank dealer said.
A slowdown in industrial demand for credit has also contributed to build up of lendable resources within the banking system, an economist with a securities firm said.

India's largest commercial bank State Bank of India reported an uptrend in demand for credit. Though other banks have not corroborated the trend, some securities firms have predicted a reversal, in October, of the industrial slowdown seen in the first half of 1996/97 (April-March).
A series of cuts in the cash reserve requirement for banks has contributed to increased deposits with the banking system, ICICI Securities and Finance Company said.
"Real estate and the stock markets are down," said the treasurer of a European bank in Bombay. "So funds are coming back to the banking system in the absence of better avenues."
